opening: Lord, meet us gently today and always
body:
The dialogue between Jesus and Peter in the Gospel of John chapter 21 happens after the crucifixion, after the empty tomb, and after Jesus has already appeared to the disciples. The setting is deeply important.
The disciples are back near the Sea of Galilee, fishing again — almost as though they are suspended between the old life and the new reality of the Resurrection. Peter, the same Peter who denied Christ three times during the Passion, now stands before the risen Christ. Then Jesus asks him three times,  “Do you love me?” And Peter answers three times. The repetition is not accidental. Peter denied Christ three times around a charcoal-burning fire..
Now Peter is given three opportunities to publicly reaffirm his love. But Jesus does something,   He restores Peter and entrusts him with the care of the Church. “Feed my lambs.” “Tend my sheep.” “Feed my sheep.” Notice they are still Christ’s sheep. Not Peter’s. Peter is being entrusted with stewardship, pastoral care, and spiritual guardianship. This passage becomes foundational in Catholic understanding of Peter’s unique role among the Apostles and ultimately the papacy. Christ is not merely forgiving Peter privately; He is publicly reaffirming and commissioning him after failure. And there is something beautiful tied to everything we discussed earlier about the Triduum and divine love; Christ does not return from death seeking revenge for betrayal. He returns, restoring communion. Peter failed dramatically during the Passion. Yet the risen Christ meets him not with destruction, but with invitation, “Do you love me?” 
The risen Christ continually calls wounded humanity back into communion with God, transforming fear, failure, suffering, and human weakness through His grace into deeper faith, surrender, and union with Him. To do his will.
